title: When an agent restyles several parts of your game at once, how do you keep it looking like one game?
author: shanebrumback
selftext:
I just had an AI agent rebuild a lot of the look of my browser shooter in one session: sky, forest, ocean, soldier, and weapon fire effects. It's a big jump, and it made me think about a problem that grows as agents take on more systems at once: keeping everything in the same visual language.

Each piece can look good on its own and still feel like it came from a different game: a painterly sky over glossy water, effects that are brighter than anything else on screen, a character lit differently from the world.

A few ideas I'm weighing, and I'd love to hear what has actually worked for you:

1. \*\*A short art-direction doc the agent reads first.\*\* Palette, time of day, how saturated effects can be, realistic vs stylized. Basically a one-page style guide.
2. \*\*Shared values instead of per-system choices.\*\* One sun direction, one fog color, one environment map that everything reads from, so the agent can't drift system by system.
3. \*\*Reference screenshots in the prompt\*\* and asking the agent to compare its render against them.
4. \*\*Changing one system at a time\*\* and reviewing before moving on, even though doing it all at once is faster.

Questions for people shipping with AI:
- Do you keep a style guide for your agents, and how specific is it?
- Has an agent ever reviewed its own screenshots well enough to catch style drift?
- Is it better to let the agent restyle everything, or lock the look early and only let it build?

Disclosure: I write about Three.js + AI on my own site. Not linking it here, I'm just interested in how others handle this.

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
I'd combine 1 and 2, and treat 2 as the one that actually holds.

A style doc helps, but agents drift from prose. Shared values in code don't drift: one lighting and fog setup, one palette file, and a cap on emissive and bloom intensity that every effect reads from. If the agent can only pick from those, a painterly sky over glossy water gets much harder to produce by accident.

For reviewing, a fixed set of camera positions captured as screenshots after every change, compared side by side with the previous set, tends to work better than asking the agent whether something matches the style. Models are decent at spotting a difference when you show them two images, and much worse at judging "does this fit" in the abstract.

And lock the look early. Restyling everything at once is fast, but then every later system has to chase a moving target.
